newsitem.title: USA: American Air, pilots negotiate as strike looms.
newsitem.headline: American Air, pilots negotiate as strike looms.

text.p: American Airlines pilots' union said on Thursday it presented new ideas to settle a labour dispute and that the two sides were "not that far apart" in negotiations to avert a damaging strike.
American, the nation's second largest airline, said it had not yet formally received a new offer from the union and was waiting to see the details before taking a position on it.

The comments were the first hints that the two sides might be toning down their harsh rhetoric in a bid to avert a strike the pilots have called for just after midnight Friday (0500 GMT Saturday) if no agreement is reached.

A strike would disrupt plans for hundreds of thousands of travelers. The Fort Worth, Tex.-based airline is trying to rebook passengers on other carriers and already has cancelled nearly all international flights scheduled on Friday night.

The union said it presented proposals on the two major issues in the negotiations -- pay for pilots on American's regular flights and whether its union pilots should fly smaller jets for the airline's American Eagle operation and their level of pay.

American wants to use lower-paid pilots from another union on the American Eagle regional flights, which the Allied Pilots Association opposes. The airline, a unit of AMR Corp., wants to lower costs to compete with other major airlines' regional commuter services.
The Allied Pilots Association said it suggested late on Wednesday that a possible compromise would be for members of their union to fly regional jets, but at lower pay.
The first reaction from American Airlines was to dismiss the offer, with a spokesman calling the suggestion "a bunch of verbiage on paper."

But American spokesman Al Comeaux later said this should not be interpreted as a rejection of the offer since the airline had not yet seen a full proposal. He said the union was expected to formally present the offer later on Thursday.
"It is our position that we have not received a proposal from the union and therefore we cannot accept or reject anything," Comeaux said.

The union's chief negotiator, Brian Mayhew, said the pilots also offered a new proposal on pay -- presumably less than the 11.5 percent pay increase over four years sought earlier -- but he gave no details.
Earlier this week, American raised its wage offer to a 6 percent raise over four years, from 5 percent, but also withdrew one of two stock option plans that had been included.
Separately, American Airlines Chairman Robert Crandall called for binding government arbitration of the dispute, a proposal the pilots have repeatedly rejected.
"I think mandatory binding arbitration should be required" to prevent airline strikes, Crandall told a congressional subcommittee.
"I seriously doubt we could accept that," union spokesman Wally Pitts said.
The two sides were already negotiating in Washington with a federal mediator present but binding arbitration would increase the government role.
Crandall told a hearing of a House Transportation subcommittee that he was unsure if a strike could be avoided.
"We have two choices: we can either cave in or take a strike. A strike of 90 days will destroy this airline."
As the talks entered their fourth day of intensive bargaining, President Bill Clinton was keeping a close watch.

Clinton could intervene and name an emergency board to try to resolve the issues. Creation of a board would prevent any work stoppages for 60 days while the board and the two parties tried again to end their differences.
But White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Thursday that Clinton wanted the two sides to work through the mediator to settle the dispute.
"He (Clinton) remains convinced that the parties should and must use the available mediation board process to address their grievances and settle their disputes," McCurry said.
The impact of a potential strike was already being felt, with travel agents steering passengers away from the airline and American trying to rebook passengers on other carriers.
Areas particularly hard hit by a strike would be the Caribbean, now at the height of its winter tourist season, and the Colorado Rockies, a popular destination for skiers.
